basicCardProfiles.flavor:
Blow of the empty fist.

The last thing a Forsaken owns once the blade is broken and the cairn has kept it. No hamlet teaches it; it is learned the first winter a sword is traded for salt.

A last resort, still yours.

Rim-blow of the Bastion's shield line.

Climbers learn it from salvaged Warden shields, once gilded with the branch. Most scrape the gold away. The corrupted Wardens of the Fell Courtyard hesitate at the sight of it.

Some leave the gold.

Plain cut of Bastion steel.

Drilled into the field levies and the sellswords hired beside them. Weald smiths never signed their blades, a custom the Chapel's scribes thought insolent and never ended.

Unsigned steel can be carried without anyone asking whose it was.

Turning flurry of the Citadel's midwinter masque.

Court dancers spun double-ended blades before the throne. Stitched to their posts when the Court Flame died, some turn yet upon the frozen river, slower each winter.

Climbers learn the step by watching. The dancers do not mind.

Two quick openings, as the Court's surgeons let a vein.

Their apprentices taught it on the docks once the Court stopped paying them. One teaches it yet, for cinders, beneath the ice below the Citadel.

He learned to open people. He taught himself to close them, and does not sell that part.

Shot loosed from low cover.

The way weald poachers took the deer the Bastion kept for its tables. The Bastion hanged poachers, so the hamlets loosed upon the dawn peal, which hid the sound of the string.

The Bell Keeper rings the peal yet, though no dawn follows.

Cold light struck from an apprentice's staff.

Cut green from weald lanternwood and tipped with starstone bought from the reach miners. The Starwatch taught that the light came from the stone.

It came more easily with the staff turned skyward. The apprentices were told not to notice.

Working of a cantor's sceptre.

Chapel sceptres bore script copied from sealstone doors older than the Chapel. The cantors were taught its sounds, never its sense. The Chapel called the script sacred.

Among themselves, the cantors called it borrowed.

Empty-handed guard of the ice-fishers.

Weight low, feet wide, upon lakes that crack all winter and hold but one at a time. The fishers of Sallow Lake say the ice has a temper, and may be reasoned with.

Those who said otherwise are beneath it.

Haft-turn of the Bastion's field levies.

Sergeant Ilse drilled it upon the Muster Stair. On quiet nights her voice carries from the Bastion walls, calling the count.

The levies she drilled are corrupted now. When they hear her, they take their places.

Shield set against the blow, as the Wardens taught.

Bastion shields bore strips of bell-bronze upon the rim, cast from metal left when the great bell was founded. The Wardens said the bronze rang the hour when struck.

It rings at other hours too.

Ward drawn through a staff, taught upon Starwatch Terrace.

Where the apprentices measured the new tower's draw across the water. The Astronomer said the ward was against the salt wind.

It leaned toward the Spire whenever it was drawn.

Ward of the bier-watch.

Cantors held a sceptre crosswise over the dead through the night, before a name was written. The Chapel taught that it kept the name from wandering.

Where a name might wander, the rubric does not say.

Art of the empty hand.

Mostly the art of not being where the blow lands, taught by the ship-breakers upon hulls that shift with the tide. Gull-Bet calls it the first thing the Forsaken ever had that the marked envied.

That has been true for a very short while.

A weapon learned as it was last used.

Take up what the corrupted drop, and let its habits show. A blade taken from a Warden cuts like a Warden. Orla of the hamlets below the Bastion bears a sword that dips toward the Fell Courtyard as she passes.

She no longer fights the pull.

The poacher's pause before loosing.

Breath out, hand set, wait for the bell. Weald poachers learned patience from the Bastion's gamekeepers, who hanged the impatient. The gamekeepers walk the lanternwood yet, among the corrupted.

They count beneath their breath. The count never ends.

Breath set behind the focus.

Counted to the rhythm of the star tables, recited until the rhythm lived in the breath. The Starwatch taught the tables were only numbers; the apprentices held the rhythm older.

On the night of the eclipse, the Astronomer read the last table aloud, and did not stop at its end.
